title: The wedding in the code
hook: the four lavan, no dowry, no child marriage

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam karan: a hukam gives the first letter, the family chooses the name, and Singh or Kaur is added. Your line was the name from the hukam. Whose name did you say with more care? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

No exchange of rings at the center of it. No vows written by the couple. No officiant asking if anyone objects. At a Sikh wedding the couple sits side by side on the floor in front of the Guru Granth Sahib, the groom's scarf in the bride's hand, linking them. A hymn is read. Then it is sung, and as it's sung the couple rises and walks slowly around the Granth, the groom ahead, the bride following, the cloth between them. They sit. Another verse is read, and they walk again. By the end, they have circled the Guru, and they are married. The whole wedding hangs on that one hymn.
screen: `NO RINGS AT THE CENTER.` → `A SCARF BETWEEN THEM.` → `WALKING AROUND THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Anand Karaj means the ceremony of bliss. Anand is bliss, the same word as the Anand Sahib we heard at the bhog, and karaj is a ceremony or an undertaking. The heart of it is the lavan, a hymn by Guru Ram Das on Ang seven hundred seventy-three of the Guru Granth Sahib, in four stanzas. Each stanza is one lav, one round. Each is read, then sung while the couple walks around the Granth. In paraphrase, the rounds move like a journey: the first is about taking up a life of duty and remembering the Name; the second about losing fear and meeting the Lord in every place; the third about longing and love in the company of the holy; the fourth about peace, the union found. Read that way, the hymn is about the soul and God, and the couple is invited to see their marriage inside that larger love. Now the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada surrounds the ceremony with rules that protect people. In paraphrase: a marriage should be arranged without regard to caste. No child marriage. No dowry. No consulting the stars for a lucky date or hour. Each of those rules removes a way a wedding can become a transaction or a burden, especially for a young bride and her family. What's left is simple: two people, the Guru, a hymn and four rounds.
screen: `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · `THE LAVAN, A HYMN IN FOUR ROUNDS.` · `A JOURNEY OF THE SOUL TO GOD.` · `NO CASTE, NO DOWRY, NO CHILD BRIDE.` · then, large: `FOUR ROUNDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish a couple well. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two people who share a life: newlyweds, your parents, friends, a couple who has been through a hard year. Picture them walking slowly together, one step behind the other, the way the couple walks the rounds. Hold them in mind and wish them steadiness, kindness, and peace between them. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. Then, if it feels right, plan to send them a short note today. The bell holds the time.
Anand Karaj. The Sikh wedding, the ceremony of bliss: the four lavan of Guru Ram Das, sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.
Your line: four rounds. Today, send one couple you know a word of good will, and keep it simple: no gift attached. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.
